A Handbook of Chronobiological Data Analysis

A practical guide to analysis techniques, integrated with AnCiR

Chronobiology — the study of biological rhythms — has generated a rich ecosystem of analytical methods spanning simple visual inspection to sophisticated statistical modelling. This handbook is a practical companion: clear enough for beginners, detailed enough for researchers, and directly tied to real analysis workflows in AnCiR (ancir.pages.dev), a free, browser-based platform requiring no installation.

How to Use This Handbook
  • Chapters are largely self-contained — jump to the method you need.
  • Each chapter opens with Historical Context, then concept, mathematics, and a step-by-step AnCiR workflow.
  • Mathematical detail can be skipped without loss of continuity.
  • Worked examples use datasets that can be generated or imported in AnCiR.
  • This handbook draws on Refinetti, Cornélissen & Halberg (2007) [1] Biological Rhythm Research 38(4):275–325.

Quick Start AnCiR Quick Start

AnCiR (Analysis of Chronobiological Rhythms) runs entirely in the browser at ancir.pages.dev. No installation, no account, no programming required.

🔬 First steps in AnCiR
  1. Open ancir.pages.dev in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari).
  2. To explore without your own data: click File → Load Example Session.
  3. To import your own data: click the import icon (↑ arrow) in the toolbar, and select a CSV or Excel (.xlsx) file.
  4. AnCiR detects column types automatically. Check the icons in the data panel: 🕐 = time, # = number, ≡ = category. Click a column header to change its type if needed.
  5. The general workflow is: Import → Column Processes → Table Processes → Plots.
  6. Save your session at any time via File → Save Session (produces a .ancir file you can reload later).
  7. Undo/redo with Cmd+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z (Mac) or Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z (Windows).
💡 Tip: Use the Workflow view (View menu) to see the entire data pipeline as a visual diagram — very useful once you have multiple processes and plots.

Core concepts

ConceptWhat it is
Column ProcessTransforms a single column in place (Add, Subtract, Normalise, Remove Trend, Remove Outliers, Filter). Non-destructive — the original data is always preserved.
Table ProcessTakes one or more input columns and produces new output columns (Cosinor, Bin Data, Smooth Data, Simulate Data, Long To Wide, etc.).
PlotVisualises data from columns (Actogram, Scatterplot, Periodogram, Correlogram, Fourier Analysis, Boxplot, Tableplot).
Stored ValuesSingle numbers produced by analyses (e.g., fitted period, amplitude) that can be referenced in Formula Columns or viewed in the Stored Values panel.
ch1:
Chapter 1 Introduction to Chronobiology

📜 Historical Context
1729 — Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan demonstrates that Mimosa pudica maintains daily leaf movements in complete darkness — the first experimental evidence of an endogenous biological clock.
1751 — Carl Linnaeus designs his "Horologium Florae" (Flower Clock), exploiting predictable daily timing of floral opening across species.
1960s–80s — Jürgen Aschoff and Colin Pittendrigh dominate the field, establishing formal rules of circadian entrainment and coining many terms still in use today.
2017 — Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the molecular mechanisms of the circadian clock.

What is a Biological Rhythm?

A biological rhythm is any periodic, self-sustaining oscillation in a physiological, biochemical, or behavioural process. Rhythms are characterised by four key parameters:

ParameterDefinition
Period (τ)The time to complete one full cycle. For circadian rhythms, τ ≈ 24 hours.
Amplitude (A)Half the peak-to-trough difference — a measure of rhythm strength.
Phase (φ)The timing of a reference point (e.g., peak or onset) relative to a fixed time.
MESOR (M)Midline Estimating Statistic Of Rhythm — the rhythm-adjusted mean level.

Biological rhythms are classified by period length. Circadian rhythms (Latin: circa diem, 'about a day') have periods of ~24 hours. Ultradian rhythms are shorter than 24 hours (e.g., REM sleep cycles ~90 min); infradian rhythms are longer (e.g., menstrual cycle ~28 days).

The Circadian Clock

Circadian rhythms are generated by endogenous molecular clocks present in virtually every cell. In mammals, the master pacemaker is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus. The molecular clockwork is built on a transcription-translation feedback loop (a process where the proteins produced by a gene gradually switch that same gene off, creating a ~24-hour cycle):

  • CLOCK and BMAL1 drive transcription of Period (PER1/2/3) and Cryptochrome (CRY1/2) genes.
  • PER and CRY proteins accumulate over several hours, then feed back to inhibit CLOCK/BMAL1 activity.
  • As PER and CRY are degraded (~24 hours), CLOCK/BMAL1-driven transcription restarts.
  • Secondary stabilising loops involving REV-ERBα/β and RORα add robustness.
📌 Key Point
The intrinsic period (free-running period, τ) is rarely exactly 24 hours — in humans the average is ~24.2 hours. Daily synchronisation (entrainment) requires external time cues called zeitgebers.

Zeitgebers and Entrainment

Zeitgebers (German: "time-givers") synchronise the internal clock to the external world. Light is the dominant zeitgeber, acting via intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) and the retinohypothalamic tract. Non-photic zeitgebers include:

  • Feeding/fasting cycles — entrain peripheral clocks (liver, gut, adipose tissue) via metabolic signals.
  • Exercise — acute physical activity can phase-shift the circadian system, timing-dependently.
  • Temperature — the primary zeitgeber for many organisms; also influences mammalian peripheral clocks.
  • Social cues — mealtimes, work schedules, and social interactions contribute to human circadian timing.

Why Circadian Biology Matters

Clinical and Medical Importance

Circadian disruption — from shift work, jet lag, hospitalisation, or social misalignment — has broad health consequences: elevated risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes in shift workers; morning peaks in myocardial infarction and stroke; associations between shift work and breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer (IARC Group 2A carcinogen). In perioperative medicine, surgery and ICU care disrupt circadian rhythms through light exposure, fasting, sedation, and inflammation, contributing to delirium, immune impairment, and delayed recovery.

Chronopharmacology and Precision Medicine

Drug efficacy and toxicity vary with time of administration. Examples: evening dosing of ACE inhibitors better suppresses nocturnal blood pressure; timed delivery of oxaliplatin and 5-fluorouracil improves chemotherapy tolerability; short-acting statins are more effective taken at night when hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks.

Research Perspective

Circadian data are inherently time-structured. Standard statistical methods that ignore temporal ordering can give misleading results. This handbook provides the foundation to choose the right analysis, estimate parameters with appropriate uncertainty, compare rhythms between conditions, and use open-source tools reproducibly.
ch2:
Chapter 2 Data Collection

📜 Historical Context
1922 — Maynard Johnson pioneers quantitative locomotor activity recording in rodents.
1960s — The Esterline-Angus event recorder enables continuous paper-tape recordings of animal activity.
1980s–90s — Wrist actigraphy devices emerge for human circadian research.
2000s–present — Miniaturised wearables and smartphone-based sensing dramatically expand scale and ecological validity.

Types of Chronobiological Data

  • Locomotor activity — running wheel counts, accelerometry, infrared beam breaks.
  • Sleep-wake state — polysomnography (PSG), actigraphy, video scoring.
  • Physiological signals — core body temperature (CBT), heart rate, blood pressure.
  • Hormonal markers — cortisol, melatonin, insulin, growth hormone at multiple time points.
  • Gene/protein expression — qPCR, RNA-seq, proteomics time-courses.

Sampling Considerations

The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem (the rule that says you need to measure at least twice as often as the rhythm cycles) states that to detect a rhythm of period τ, data must be sampled at least twice per period (sampling interval ≤ τ/2). For circadian rhythms, 1–4 hourly sampling is standard for hormone assays; wearables typically sample at 30-second to 1-minute resolution.

⚠️ Sparse Sampling
With fewer than 6 time points per 24-hour cycle, many standard analyses become unreliable. Methods designed for sparse or unevenly-spaced data — the Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] periodogram and cosinor regression — should be preferred. At minimum, 5–7 complete cycles are recommended for reliable period estimation.

File Formats

AnCiR accepts CSV and Excel (.xlsx) files. The minimum requirement is a timestamp column and one or more data columns. Timestamps can be provided as absolute datetime, elapsed time in hours/minutes, or Zeitgeber Time (ZT) / Circadian Time (CT).

🔬 Importing Data into AnCiR
  1. Go to ancir.pages.dev — no installation needed.
  2. Click the import icon (↑) in the top toolbar, or drag and drop your file onto the page.
  3. Select your CSV or Excel (.xlsx) file. AnCiR reads both formats automatically.
  4. AnCiR detects column types automatically. In the data panel, check that your time column has the clock (🕐) icon. If it was mis-detected, click the column header and select "Time".
  5. Time columns are shown in hours-since-start for analysis internally — you don't need to convert them manually.
  6. To explore the tool without your own data, choose File → Load Example Session instead.
💡 Multiple animals or subjects: You can import all data in one file using a category column (e.g., "Subject ID"). The Long To Wide table process can then split them into per-subject columns for analysis.
ch3:
Chapter 3 Simulating Chronobiological Data

📜 Historical Context
1970s–80s — As the field developed increasingly complex analytical tools, simulated data became essential for validation and benchmarking.
Refinetti et al. (2007) provided the most comprehensive framework for simulating chronobiological data, including guidelines on period, amplitude, noise, and waveform shape.

Why Simulate Data?

Simulated data serve several purposes: testing whether an analysis method correctly recovers known parameters; teaching students how analytical tools behave; benchmarking new software; and exploring how noise, sampling rate, or missing data affect results.

The Basic Sinusoidal Model

The simplest model of a circadian rhythm is a sinusoidal oscillation with added noise:

\[ y(t) = M + A \cdot \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau} + \phi\right) + \varepsilon(t) \]

Where M is the MESOR, A is the amplitude, τ is the period, φ is the phase offset, and ε(t) ~ N(0, σ²) is random noise. Real biological rhythms are rarely perfectly sinusoidal — more realistic simulations may use truncated sinusoids, Poisson noise (for count data), or gradual period drift.

🔬 Generating Simulated Data in AnCiR
  1. In the data panel, click Add Table Process and select Simulate Data.
  2. Set the Start Time and date (e.g., 2024-01-01 00:00) and the Sampling Interval (e.g., 0.25 h for 15-minute resolution).
  3. Add one or more Sections: each section defines a phase of recording with its own Period (h), Amplitude, and Phase offset (h). Using multiple sections lets you simulate a free-running rhythm that shifts partway through.
  4. Click Run. Two new columns appear: a timestamp column and a values column.
  5. Proceed to create an Actogram or Periodogram directly from these columns.
💡 Use Simulate Data to verify your analysis pipeline: if you generate data with a known period of exactly 24.0 h, the periodogram and cosinor should recover 24.0 h — if they don't, something is wrong with the pipeline.
ch4:
Chapter 4 Preprocessing

📜 Historical Context
Pre-digital era — Preprocessing was performed manually: researchers visually inspected paper records, hand-marked artefacts, and calculated summary statistics by hand.
1980s–90s — Digital data enabled automated preprocessing but also introduced new artefacts (recording dropouts, sensor drift) requiring new approaches.

Preprocessing — the steps taken before formal analysis — can dramatically affect results. The goal is to improve signal quality without introducing bias. Document every preprocessing decision: choices made here can strongly influence downstream results.

Outlier Removal

Common approaches include threshold-based flagging (values exceeding mean ± k·SD, typically k = 3) or the more robust median absolute deviation (MAD) method.

Threshold = mean(y) + 3 · SD(y)

Missing data created by outlier removal can propagate through analyses. For spectral methods, methods designed to work with missing data points (e.g., Lomb [3]-Scargle [4]) are preferable to simple deletion or interpolation.

🔬 Removing Outliers in AnCiR (Column Process)
  1. In the data panel, click the + (Add Process) button on the column you want to clean.
  2. Select Remove Outliers.
  3. Choose the method: IQR (values outside Q1 − 1.5·IQR or Q3 + 1.5·IQR) or Z-Score (default: |z| > 3).
  4. Adjust the threshold if needed, then click Apply.
  5. Outlier values are replaced with null. The list of removed values and their row positions is shown in the process panel.

Binning

High-resolution data are aggregated into coarser intervals. A bin width of τ/48 to τ/96 (15–30 min for a 24-hour rhythm) is generally appropriate.

y_binned[i] = mean(y[i·w : (i+1)·w]) — for continuous data y_binned[i] = sum(y[i·w : (i+1)·w]) — for count data (e.g., wheel turns)
🔬 Binning Data in AnCiR (Table Process)
  1. Click Add Table Process and select Bin Data.
  2. Select your Time column (X) and data column(s) (Y). Multiple Y columns can be binned in one step.
  3. Set the Bin size (e.g., 1 h) and Bin start offset.
  4. Choose the aggregation function: Mean (for continuous measurements), Sum (for count data such as wheel revolutions), Median, Min, Max, or SD.
  5. Optionally set a different Step size (< bin size) to create a sliding-window average with overlapping bins.
  6. Click Run. New binned X and Y columns appear in the data panel.

Smoothing

Smoothing reduces high-frequency noise. For periodogram analysis, smoothing with a window corresponding to ~1–2 bin widths is typically sufficient.

MethodDescriptionKey parameter
Moving AverageArithmetic, weighted, or exponential mean over a sliding windowWindow size; type (simple/weighted/exponential)
Savitzky-GolayFits a polynomial to each window — preserves peaks better than plain averagingWindow size; polynomial degree
LOESSLocally weighted regression — very flexible, handles irregular samplingBandwidth (fraction of data used per local fit)
Whittaker-EilersPenalised least squares — excellent for uniformly sampled biological data; handles gapsλ (smoothness penalty); order (default 2)
🔬 Smoothing Data in AnCiR (Table Process)
  1. Click Add Table Process and select Smooth Data.
  2. Select the X (time) and Y column(s). Multiple Y columns can be smoothed in one step.
  3. Choose a smoothing method and set its parameters. Whittaker-Eilers with λ = 100 works well for most circadian recordings.
  4. Click Run. New smoothed X and Y columns appear.
  5. Use these smoothed columns as input for your Actogram or Periodogram.

Removing Trend (Detrending)

Many biological recordings have a slow non-rhythmic drift (animal weight gain, sensor drift, masking effects). Detrending removes this baseline drift and is recommended before cosinor analysis and periodogram computation when a trend is present.

🔬 Detrending in AnCiR (Column Process)
  1. Click + (Add Process) on the column you want to detrend.
  2. Select Remove Trend.
  3. Choose the trend model: Linear is sufficient for most recordings. Polynomial (with configurable degree), Exponential, and Logarithmic options are available for more complex drifts.
  4. Click Apply. The displayed column values are now the residuals (original − fitted trend). The fitted equation, R², and RMSE are shown in the process panel.
  5. The original data is always preserved — you can remove this process to restore it.
ch5:
Chapter 5 Actograms

📜 Historical Context
1922 — Maynard Johnson creates the first recognisably modern actograms, plotting locomotor activity of deer mice over consecutive days.
1950s–60s — Colin Pittendrigh popularises the double-plotted actogram, displaying two consecutive 24-hour cycles side by side on each row — invaluable for revealing free-running rhythms.
1960s — Esterline-Angus event recorders enable continuous paper records; actograms were produced by physically cutting and re-aligning paper tapes.
Present — Web-based platforms including AnCiR make actogram generation accessible without any software installation.

Actograms are the fundamental visualisation tool of chronobiology. They display activity data across multiple days in a stacked format that makes temporal patterns immediately visible — periodicity, phase shifts, entrainment, and free-running rhythms all become apparent at a glance.

How an Actogram Works

Time-series data are "folded" into cycles of the assumed period (typically 24 hours). Each cycle occupies one horizontal row, with time on the x-axis and activity on the y-axis. Days are stacked top-to-bottom. Vertical bars represent the magnitude of activity at each time point.

Double-Plotting

In a double-plotted actogram, each row displays two consecutive cycles side by side. This is the standard format in chronobiology. When the endogenous period is not exactly 24 hours, activity onsets drift systematically across rows — rightward for τ > 24 h, leftward for τ < 24 h — and double-plotting makes this drift easy to see by providing visual continuity.

What Actograms Reveal

  • Periodicity — whether a rhythm repeats consistently every ~24 hours.
  • Phase shifts — changes in the timing of activity onset or offset due to jet lag, shifted light-dark cycles, or experimental manipulations.
  • Entrainment — stable onset times relative to the zeitgeber indicate successful synchronisation.
  • Free-running rhythms — in constant conditions (DD or LL), the endogenous period is revealed by systematic onset drift.
  • Arrhythmicity — absence of rhythmic patterning, seen in clock-mutant animals or severe disruption.

Mathematics

Data Folding

For timestamps t₁, t₂, …, tₙ and folding period τ, the row number and position within row for the i-th data point are:

\[ \text{Row} = \left\lfloor \frac{t_i}{\tau} \right\rfloor, \qquad \text{Position within row} = t_i \bmod \tau \]

Period Estimation from Onset Times

Activity onsets are detected as the first time per cycle that y exceeds a threshold:

Threshold = mean(y) + k · SD(y) Onset[c] = first t where y(t) > threshold, within cycle c

The period is estimated from the slope of a linear regression of onset time on cycle number: τ̂ = 24 + slope (slope in hours per cycle).

Worked Example

Simulated rodent locomotor activity: 15-minute resolution over 28 days in DD. Days 1–14: τ = 24.5 h (rightward drift); days 15–28: τ = 22.25 h (leftward drift). Signal: Activity = 50 + 50 · sin(2πt/τ) + Uniform(0,10) noise. The actogram immediately reveals the change at day 14. Automated onset detection with threshold = mean + 1·SD, followed by linear regression, yields τ̂ = 24.52 h for days 1–14 and τ̂ = 22.28 h for days 15–28.

🔬 Creating an Actogram in AnCiR
  1. Click Add Plot (the plot icon in the toolbar) and select Actogram.
  2. Choose your Time column and Values column from the dropdowns.
  3. Set the Period (default: 24 h) — this sets how many hours fit in each horizontal row.
  4. Set the Start Time — the hour of day at which each row begins. For a standard actogram starting at midnight, use 0; for one starting at lights-on (e.g. 06:00), use 6.
  5. Enable Double plot to show two consecutive cycles per row — the standard format in chronobiology.
  6. Light bands: enable and enter the light period start and end (in hours from the row start) to shade the light phase. E.g., for a 12:12 LD cycle with lights on at row start, enter start = 0 and end = 12.
  7. Phase markers: enable to automatically draw a marker at activity onset or offset each day. Adjust the threshold using the slider.
  8. Resize the plot by dragging its corners. Export as PNG or SVG using the download icon above the plot.
💡 If onset markers seem incorrect, try adjusting the threshold. A threshold around mean + 0.5–1.5·SD usually works well for locomotor activity data.
ch6:
Chapter 6 Periodograms

📜 Historical Context
1965 — James Enright introduces the χ² periodogram to chronobiology, providing the first objective test for rhythmicity in locomotor activity data.
1978 — Philip Sokolove and Wayne Bushell refine and popularise the chi-square periodogram with a clear mathematical framework still used today (J. Theor. Biol. 72:131–160).
1975–76 — Nicholas Lomb [3] and Jeffrey Scargle [4] independently develop the Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] periodogram for handling irregularly spaced data.

A periodogram provides an objective, quantitative assessment of rhythmic structure by estimating the relative contribution of different periodicities to an observed time series. The result is a plot of spectral power (a measure of how strongly each period contributes to the signal) against period, with significant peaks identifying dominant rhythms.

Chi-Squared Periodogram (Sokolove-Bushell)

The most widely used method in chronobiology. For each test period P, data are folded and the χ² statistic tests whether bin means differ from the grand mean:

Qₚ = (N/k) · Σⱼ (x̄ⱼ − x̄)² / s²

Where N is the total data points, k is bins per fold, x̄ⱼ is the mean of bin j, x̄ is the grand mean, and s² is the overall variance. Q_p is approximately χ²-distributed with (k−1) degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis of no rhythmicity.

⚠️ Important Limitation
The χ² periodogram requires equally spaced data. For sparse or irregularly sampled data (e.g., clinical hormone assays), use the Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] periodogram instead.

Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] Periodogram

Handles irregularly sampled time series by fitting sinusoidal models at each test frequency, correcting for unequal spacing via a phase offset parameter. Increasingly used in chronobiology for sparse clinical datasets, actigraphy with gaps, and hormone time-course data.

Enright (Autocorrelation) Periodogram

Uses the autocorrelation function at each candidate period. An alternative to Chi-squared that is robust with longer recordings and requires no distributional assumptions.

Interpreting a Periodogram

  • A sharp, high-power peak at ~24 h indicates well-entrained circadian rhythmicity.
  • In free-running conditions, the peak shifts to the animal's endogenous τ.
  • Multiple peaks may indicate harmonic structure (at τ/2, τ/3) or genuine multi-frequency rhythmicity.
  • A flat periodogram suggests arrhythmicity, insufficient data, or excessive noise.
⚠️ Harmonic Artefact
The chi-squared periodogram may identify a spurious 12 h component in square-wave data (Refinetti et al. 2007, Fig. 16). If you see a 12 h peak alongside the 24 h peak, confirm with Lomb [3]-Scargle [4].
🔬 Running a Periodogram in AnCiR
  1. Click Add Plot and select Periodogram.
  2. Choose your Time column and Data column.
  3. Select the method:
    • Chi-squared (Sokolove-Bushell) — best for regularly sampled activity data; most widely used in chronobiology.
    • Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] — use for data with irregular timing or gaps.
    • Enright (autocorrelation) — robust alternative to Chi-squared for longer recordings.
  4. Set the period range to test (e.g., 16–32 h for circadian analysis; widen for ultradian/infradian).
  5. For Chi-squared and Enright, set the Bin size (e.g., 0.5–1 h).
  6. Set the significance level α (default 0.05). A significance threshold line is drawn automatically across the plot.
  7. The dominant peak period and its power value are shown in the statistics panel below the plot.
  8. Hover over the plot to read off the exact period and power at any point.
💡 Note the estimated period for use in the next step — Cosinor analysis performs better when you use the measured τ rather than assuming exactly 24 h.
ch7:
Chapter 7 Cosinor Analysis

📜 Historical Context
1950s–60s — Franz Halberg (University of Minnesota) develops cosinor analysis as a principled way to estimate rhythm parameters from clinical and physiological data. Halberg also coined the term "circadian".
1967 — Halberg formally describes the cosinor method; it rapidly becomes the standard for quantifying circadian parameters in human studies.
1970s–80s — The population-mean cosinor extension is developed, enabling group-level inference across multiple subjects.
Present — Cosinor analysis is implemented in cosinor2 (R), CircadiPy (Python), BioDare2 (web), and AnCiR.

Cosinor analysis is a regression-based method for characterising rhythms. Unlike periodograms, which detect whether a rhythm exists, cosinor analysis estimates rhythm parameters — MESOR, amplitude, and acrophase — with confidence intervals, enabling formal comparison between groups or conditions.

The Cosinor Model

A rhythm is modelled as a cosine function fitted by linear regression. By substituting β = A·cos(φ) and γ = −A·sin(φ):

\[ y(t) = M + \beta\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau}\right) + \gamma\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau}\right) + \varepsilon(t) \]

This is linear in β and γ and is fitted by ordinary least squares. The rhythm parameters are recovered as:

\[ A = \sqrt{\beta^2 + \gamma^2}, \qquad \phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{-\gamma}{\beta}\right) \]
ParameterMeaningUnits
MESOR (M)Rhythm-adjusted mean — the midline of the fitted cosineSame as y
Amplitude (A)Half the peak-to-trough excursion of the rhythmSame as y
Acrophase (φ)Time of peak (clock time or hours from ZT0)Hours
Period (τ)Duration of one cycle — fixed or free to varyHours

Fixed-Period vs. Free-Parameter Mode

When the period is known (e.g., studying a circadian rhythm in LD conditions), fixed-period (Halberg) cosinor is preferred — it gives more robust parameter estimates with confidence intervals and an F-test for rhythm significance. When the period is unknown, free-parameter mode fits the period alongside amplitude and phase.

Population-Mean Cosinor

When multiple subjects have been recorded, the population-mean cosinor estimates group-level rhythm parameters by vector-averaging individual (β, γ) estimates, tested using the modified F-test (Bingham et al.). In AnCiR, use Collect Columns or Long To Wide with a nested Cosinor table process to run cosinor on multiple subjects at once and download the results table.

🔬 Cosinor Analysis in AnCiR
  1. Click Add Table Process and select Cosinor.
  2. Choose your Time column (X) and one or more data columns (Y). Multiple Y columns are fitted independently in one step.
  3. Choose mode:
    • Fixed-period (Halberg cosinor): enter the period (use 24 h, or your estimated τ from the periodogram). Set the number of harmonics (start with 1). This gives MESOR, amplitude, acrophase ± 95% CI, and an F-test p-value.
    • Free-parameter: set N = 1 to fit a single sinusoid with optimised period and phase. N > 1 fits multiple overlapping cosines.
  4. Optionally select an Output X column (a Sequence Column with regular spacing) to evaluate the fitted curve at fine intervals for a smooth overlay plot.
  5. Click Run. New fitted X and Y columns appear in the data panel.
  6. Overlay the fit: click Add Plot → Scatterplot. Add the raw data as Series 1 (points). Add the fitted columns as Series 2 (line, no points). This shows the fitted curve over your data.
  7. View MESOR, amplitude, acrophase, R², and p-value in the table process statistics panel.
  8. Click Store next to any statistic (e.g., period, amplitude) to save it as a Stored Value for use in Formula Columns or the Stored Values display.
💡 Best practice: Detrend the data first (Remove Trend column process) if there is a slow baseline drift, then bin or smooth before fitting the cosinor.
ch8:
Chapter 8 Fourier Analysis

📜 Historical Context
1822 — Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier shows that any periodic function can be expressed as a sum of sinusoids — the theoretical foundation of all spectral analysis.
1965 — James Cooley and John Tukey publish the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm, reducing computational cost from O(N²) to O(N log N) (from slow to fast for large datasets) and enabling practical spectral analysis of long time series.
1970s — Fourier-based power spectrum analysis is adopted in chronobiology alongside the χ² periodogram.

Core Concept

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) decomposes a time series into constituent frequency components. For N discretely sampled points with sampling interval Δt:

Fⱼ = Σᵢ xᵢ · e^(−2πi·j·i/N)

The power spectrum |Fⱼ|² plotted against period (1/fⱼ) reveals dominant rhythmic components. AnCiR uses the Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm and zero-pads data to the next power of 2 for computational efficiency.

Windowing

When the true rhythm period is not a precise multiple of the record length, spectral power "leaks" to adjacent frequencies. Windowing functions (Hann, Hamming, Blackman) reduce spectral leakage (where power from one frequency 'bleeds' into neighbouring frequencies) at the cost of some frequency resolution.

Important Limitation

⚠️ Requires Uniform Sampling
FFT assumes uniformly sampled data. For irregularly sampled data or recordings with gaps, use the Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] periodogram (Chapter 6) instead. Fourier frequency resolution = 1/T, so records shorter than ~5 cycles have too coarse a resolution to separate closely spaced periods.
🔬 Fourier Analysis in AnCiR
  1. Click Add Plot and select Fourier Analysis.
  2. Choose your Time column and Data column. Ensure the data are uniformly sampled (use Bin Data first if needed).
  3. The magnitude spectrum (√power) is plotted against period in hours. Peaks correspond to dominant oscillatory components.
  4. Hover over a peak to read off its period. The primary peak is highlighted automatically.
  5. Note: for irregularly sampled or gappy data, use the Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] Periodogram instead.
ch9:
Chapter 9 Correlograms

📜 Historical Context
1954 — Norbert Wiener and others formalise the autocorrelation function for signal analysis — a foundation quickly adopted in biological rhythm research.
1990s — Non-parametric circadian rhythm analysis (NPCRA) metrics including Interdaily Stability (IS) and Intradaily Variability (IV) are developed for actigraphic data in clinical and ageing research (van Someren et al. [10]).

The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures the correlation of a time series with a time-lagged version of itself. A correlogram (ACF vs. lag) detects rhythmicity and estimates period without the distributional assumptions of spectral methods.

The Autocorrelation Function

\[ r(k) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_i \left(y_i - \bar{y}\right)\left(y_{i+k} - \bar{y}\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_i \left(y_i - \bar{y}\right)^2} \]

For a 24-hour rhythm, significant positive peaks are expected at lags of approximately 24, 48, and 72 hours. The decay of peak height across lags reflects rhythm stability and noise.

Period Estimation

\[ \hat{\tau} = k_{\text{peak}} \cdot \Delta t \quad \text{(first ACF peak lag} \times \text{sampling interval)} \]

This approach is robust to moderate noise. If no clear peak appears within the circadian range, this suggests arrhythmicity or signal-to-noise too low for reliable detection.

Interdaily Stability and Intradaily Variability

These metrics are particularly useful in clinical populations (older adults, ICU patients, dementia) where traditional period estimation may be unreliable due to irregular activity patterns.

MetricWhat it measuresRange
Interdaily Stability (IS)Fraction of total variance explained by the average 24-hour pattern — a measure of how regular the daily rhythm is across multiple days0 (no regularity) to 1 (perfect)
Intradaily Variability (IV)Mean squared difference between consecutive time points relative to overall variance — a measure of within-day fragmentation0 (smooth) to 2 (highly fragmented)
🔬 Creating a Correlogram in AnCiR
  1. Click Add Plot and select Correlogram.
  2. Choose your Time column and Data column.
  3. The autocorrelation function is plotted against lag (in hours).
  4. Significant peaks at 24, 48, 72 h confirm circadian rhythmicity. The lag of the first major positive peak after zero estimates τ.
  5. Interdaily Stability (IS) and Intradaily Variability (IV) are calculated automatically and shown in the statistics panel below the plot.
  6. Adjust the maximum lag range to inspect ultradian structure (< 24 h) or multi-day rhythms (> 24 h).
ch10:
Chapter 10 Phase Response Curves

📜 Historical Context
1954 — Colin Pittendrigh constructs the first formal phase response curves (PRCs) for light pulses in Drosophila — demonstrating that the effect of a zeitgeber depends critically on when in the cycle it is applied.
1980s–90s — Human PRCs for light (Czeisler, Kronauer) and melatonin (Lewy) are constructed using carefully controlled laboratory studies, enabling clinical applications in jet lag, shift work, and delayed sleep-wake phase disorder.
Present — PRCs have been characterised for light, melatonin, exercise, temperature, and feeding across many organisms, with increasing clinical application in timed light therapy and chronobiotic treatments.

Overview

A phase response curve (PRC) describes how the timing (phase) of a circadian rhythm shifts in response to a stimulus applied at different phases of the clock. PRCs are essential for predicting entrainment, understanding zeitgeber action, and designing clinical interventions such as timed light therapy or melatonin administration.

Types of PRCs

  • Type 1 (weak) PRCs — smooth, continuous phase shifts; small advances and delays. Produced by most environmental zeitgebers at moderate intensities.
  • Type 0 (strong) PRCs — large phase shifts that can reset the clock to any phase regardless of initial state. Produced by intense stimuli (bright light, certain pharmacological agents).

Constructing a PRC

Animals in constant conditions receive a brief stimulus at different circadian times (CT). The resulting phase shift (ΔΦ) is plotted against the CT of stimulation. For light PRCs: phase delays occur in the early subjective night; phase advances in the late subjective night/early morning; the subjective day is relatively insensitive ("dead zone").

📌 Human Clinical Relevance
Human light and melatonin PRCs have direct clinical relevance — they underpin timing protocols for jet lag recovery, shift-work adaptation, delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, and seasonal affective disorder treatment.
🔬 Phase Response Curves in AnCiR

PRC analysis is not yet implemented as a dedicated module in AnCiR. To construct a PRC manually:

  1. Import your data with columns: Stimulus CT (circadian time of stimulus, in hours) and Phase Shift (Δhours, positive = advance, negative = delay).
  2. Create a Scatterplot with Stimulus CT on the X axis and Phase Shift on the Y axis.
  3. Add a Smooth Data table process (LOESS or Whittaker-Eilers) to produce a smooth PRC curve overlay.
  4. To overlay multiple PRCs (e.g., different stimulus intensities), add each as a separate data series in the same Scatterplot.
💡 For formal PRC construction and Type 0/1 classification, dedicated tools such as the R package zeitgebr or BioDare2 are recommended.
ch11:
Chapter 11 General Linear and Additive Models

📜 Historical Context
1990s — Linear mixed-effects models (LMEMs) provide a natural framework for multi-subject chronobiological studies. R packages nlme and later lme4 make these methods accessible.
2000s–present — Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) with cyclic smooths are applied to circadian data to handle non-sinusoidal waveforms. LASSO and ridge regression enable high-dimensional circadian omics analysis.

Mixed-Effects Cosine Models

For repeated measures from multiple subjects, a linear mixed-effects model incorporating cosine predictors provides a powerful approach:

\[ y(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau}\right) + \beta_2\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau}\right) + \text{group}[\cdots] + (1|\text{subject}) + \varepsilon \]

The random intercept (1|subject) accounts for between-subject variability. Fixed effects can include group membership, continuous covariates (age, BMI), and interactions. Implemented in R via lme4; in Python via statsmodels.

Generalised Additive Models (GAMs)

GAMs replace linear predictors with smooth functions estimated from the data. A cyclic cubic spline smoother — enforcing continuity at the 24-hour boundary — captures complex non-sinusoidal waveforms:

\[ y(t) = f(t \bmod 24) + \text{covariates} + \varepsilon \]

GAMs are particularly useful for hormone data with sharp peaks, or activity data with extended rest bouts deviating substantially from a cosine. Implemented in R via mgcv.

🔬 Linear/Additive Models in AnCiR

Formal mixed-effects cosine models and GAMs are not currently implemented in AnCiR. However, AnCiR provides several tools for related analyses:

  1. Cosinor (fixed-period, multiple harmonics) — approximates a GAM for the circadian component. Use 2–3 harmonics for non-sinusoidal waveforms.
  2. Collect Columns or Long To Wide with nested Cosinor — runs individual cosinor fits on all subjects at once and downloads a statistics table for further analysis in R.
  3. Smooth Data (LOESS) — produces a non-parametric smooth of the data, useful for exploring non-sinusoidal shape before fitting a parametric model.
  4. For full mixed-effects modelling, export your data from AnCiR (click the download icon on any Data View plot) and use R (lme4) or Python (statsmodels).
ch12:
Chapter 12 Circular Statistics

📜 Historical Context
1953 — R.A. Fisher [13] publishes foundational work on the statistics of circular distributions.
1981 — Kanti Mardia and Peter Jupp's textbook Directional Statistics provides a comprehensive treatment, still the standard reference.
1990s–present — Circular statistics are increasingly applied in chronobiology for acrophase distributions, activity onset times, and sleep timing data. R packages circular and CircStats implement these methods.

Phase angles — acrophases, activity onset times, peak cortisol times — are circular variables that wrap around at 360° or 24 hours. Standard linear statistics (mean, SD, t-test) are inappropriate and give misleading results for circular data. Circular statistics provide the correct framework.

Descriptive Circular Statistics

\[ \bar{C} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \cos\theta_i, \qquad \bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \sin\theta_i \] \[ \bar{\theta} = \operatorname{arctan2}(\bar{S},\,\bar{C}), \qquad R = \sqrt{\bar{C}^2 + \bar{S}^2} \quad (0 \leq R \leq 1) \]

R = 1 means all phases are identical; R = 0 means phases are uniformly distributed. Circular variance = 1 − R.

Tests for Circular Data

  • Rayleigh test — tests whether phases are uniformly distributed (no preferred direction). Significant if R is large relative to n.
  • Watson-Williams test — analogous to the two-sample t-test; tests whether two groups differ significantly in mean phase.
  • Watson U² test — non-parametric test for whether two samples come from the same circular distribution.
🔬 Circular Statistics in AnCiR

A dedicated circular statistics module is not currently in AnCiR. For acrophase data from Cosinor fits:

  1. Use Collect Columns + Cosinor to obtain acrophase values for multiple subjects.
  2. Download the results table via a Data View plot linked to the Cosinor statistics table.
  3. Import the acrophase column into R (circular package) or Python (pingouin) for Rayleigh test, circular mean, and Watson-Williams group comparison.
  4. Alternatively, use BioDare2 (biodare2.ed.ac.uk) for circular statistics on acrophase data.
💡 Never use a standard unpaired t-test to compare acrophase times between groups — use the Watson-Williams test (the circular analogue of the t-test). A 23:00 acrophase and a 01:00 acrophase are only 2 hours apart circularly, but would appear 22 hours apart to a linear test.
ch13:
Chapter 13 Best Practices and Reporting

Choosing the Right Method

MethodBest suited for
ActogramVisual inspection, quality control, detecting phase shifts and free-running rhythms
χ² PeriodogramPeriod detection in dense, equally-spaced activity/locomotor data
Lomb [3]-Scargle [4]Period detection in sparse, irregularly-spaced or clinical data
Cosinor (fixed-period)Parameter estimation (amplitude, phase, MESOR) with CIs; group comparison
Cosinor (free-parameter)Exploratory period estimation when τ is not known in advance
Mixed-effects cosinorMulti-subject clinical studies with covariates
GAM (cyclic spline)Non-sinusoidal waveforms; exploratory analysis
NPCRA (IS, IV)Actigraphy in clinical populations; rhythm fragmentation assessment
Circular statisticsComparing phase angles between groups

Recommended Analysis Workflow for Actigraphy Data

🔬 Standard Actigraphy Pipeline in AnCiR
  1. Import your data (time column + activity counts column).
  2. Inspect visually: create a Scatterplot of raw data and a first Actogram to check data quality.
  3. Remove outliers (Column Process: Remove Outliers) if there are implausible spikes.
  4. Detrend (Column Process: Remove Trend, Linear) if there is a slow baseline drift.
  5. Bin if needed (Table Process: Bin Data, e.g., 15-minute bins, Mean) to reduce noise and regularise sampling.
  6. Actogram: create the main actogram with double-plotting and light-dark shading.
  7. Periodogram: run Chi-squared periodogram to confirm the dominant period and estimate τ.
  8. Cosinor: apply Cosinor (fixed-period = τ from step 7, or 24 h) to extract MESOR, amplitude, and acrophase with 95% confidence intervals.
  9. Store key results (period, amplitude, acrophase) as stored values for reporting.

Common Pitfalls

⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid
  • Analysing raw, unpreprocessed data — always inspect and preprocess before formal analysis.
  • Assuming τ = exactly 24 h — always estimate τ from the periodogram; even a 0.5 h error matters for cosinor acrophase estimates.
  • χ² periodogram on sparse or irregular data — use Lomb [3]-Scargle [4] instead.
  • Linear statistics on circular phase data — use circular statistics for acrophase comparisons between groups.
  • Insufficient recording duration — at minimum 5–7 complete cycles are needed for reliable period estimation.
  • Chi-squared harmonics in square-wave data — may produce a spurious 12 h peak. Confirm with Lomb [3]-Scargle [4].
  • Time-unspecified group comparisons — comparing groups at uncontrolled times without accounting for circadian variation can reverse effect directions (Refinetti et al. 2007, Fig. 26).
  • Ignoring masking — acute environmental effects can temporarily obscure the underlying rhythm.

Reporting Standards

When reporting chronobiological analyses, include:

  • Data type, recording duration, and sampling resolution.
  • Preprocessing steps (outlier removal, binning, smoothing) with parameters.
  • Analysis method and software, including version and citation.
  • Estimated period τ with 95% confidence interval.
  • Cosinor parameters (MESOR, amplitude, acrophase) with 95% CIs, if applicable.
  • Sample size; whether values represent group means or individual estimates.
  • Statistical tests for group comparisons, with effect sizes and p-values.
📌 Reporting Acrophase
For group comparisons of acrophase, polar plots provide an intuitive summary (amplitude = vector length, acrophase = vector angle). The 95% confidence ellipse shows joint uncertainty. For population-mean cosinor, individual vectors are plotted with the group mean vector and confidence region (Refinetti et al. 2007, Fig. 22).
glossary:
Appendix A Glossary

AcrophaseThe time at which a rhythm reaches its maximum. Expressed as a clock time or in hours from a reference point (e.g., lights-on).
AmplitudeHalf the peak-to-trough excursion of a rhythm. (Some authors use "amplitude" for the full excursion — be aware of this ambiguity.)
AutocorrelationThe correlation of a signal with a time-shifted version of itself.
Circadian rhythmA biological oscillation with a period close to 24 hours, generated by an endogenous clock.
Duty cycleThe fraction of one period that a rectangular wave spends in the "high" state.
EntrainmentThe synchronisation of an endogenous biological rhythm to an external zeitgeber cycle.
Free-running period (τ)The period of a circadian rhythm in constant conditions (no external time cues).
Infradian rhythmA biological oscillation with a period longer than 24 hours (e.g., menstrual cycle, seasonal rhythm).
IS (Interdaily Stability)The fraction of total variance explained by the average 24-hour pattern; 0 (no regularity) to 1 (perfect).
IV (Intradaily Variability)Mean squared difference between consecutive time points relative to overall variance; a measure of rhythm fragmentation.
MESORMidline Estimating Statistic Of Rhythm — the mean level of the fitted cosine curve; the rhythm-adjusted mean.
Period (τ)The duration of one complete cycle of a rhythm (usually in hours).
PhaseThe timing of a rhythm relative to a reference point (e.g., the time of peak activity).
Phase shift (ΔΦ)A change in the timing of a rhythm in response to a stimulus.
PRCPhase Response Curve — describes how phase shifts depend on the timing of a stimulus within the circadian cycle.
SCNSuprachiasmatic nucleus — the master pacemaker of the mammalian circadian system, located in the anterior hypothalamus.
Ultradian rhythmA biological oscillation with a period shorter than 24 hours (e.g., REM sleep cycles ~90 min).
Zeitgeber (ZT)An environmental time cue (literally "time-giver") that synchronises a biological clock. ZT0 is typically defined as lights-on.
